sources.title: Florence Pugh (Wikipedia article, read 2026-10-04)
sources.speaker: Wikipedia contributors
sources.locator: Lead; Early life; Career (Early roles; Breakthrough); Public image; Personal life and other work; Accolades
sources.excerpt: Florence Pugh was born on 3 January 1996 in Oxford to dancer Deborah and restaurateur Clinton Pugh. She has three siblings: actor and musician Toby Sebastian, actress Arabella Gibbins, and Rafaela "Raffie" Pugh. She suffered from tracheomalacia (a windpipe condition causing breathing problems) as a child, which led to frequent hospitalisations. The family relocated to Manilva in Spain when Pugh was three years old, hoping the warmer weather would improve her health. They lived there until she was six, when they moved back to Oxford. [...] Zach Braff's drama film A Good Person (2023), in which Pugh starred as a car crash survivor, marked her first producing venture. Instead of opting for a wig, Pugh cut off her own hair for the part. [...] She insisted on filming the scene where Belova jumps from the top of Merdeka 118 without using stunt doubles. Marvel Studios was initially reluctant to allow Pugh to perform the stunt due to insurance concerns, but after her persistent efforts, including discussions with Kevin Feige, she was permitted to perform the jump. [...] From 2019 to 2022, Pugh was in a relationship with American actor and filmmaker Zach Braff. [...] She has been dating the British actor Finn Cole since 2024. Pugh has polycystic ovary syndrome and endometriosis.
sources.context: Tertiary summary used only for biographical scaffolding (birth, family, filmography, accolades, release slate). Fetched as plaintext via the MediaWiki API on 2026-10-04. The DWD "allegedly clashed with Wilde" sentence is an allegation and must not be relied on. Lists Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026) among her Yelena films and upcoming East of Eden, Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three. Not independent evidence of motive.

sources.title: Florence Pugh Felt Acting Was a 'Massive Mistake' After Execs Criticized Her Body at 19: They Tried to Change the 'Shape of My Face'
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, quoted from an interview with The Telegraph; article by Zack Sharf (Variety)
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs 2-6
sources.excerpt: “I felt very lucky and grateful, and couldn’t believe that I had got this top-of-the-game job,” [...] “All the things that they were trying to change about me – whether it was my weight, my look, the shape of my face, the shape of my eyebrows – that was so not what I wanted to do, or the industry I wanted to work in,” Pugh said. “I’d thought the film business would be like [my experience of making] ‘The Falling,’ but actually, this was what the top of the game looked like, and I felt I’d made a massive mistake.” [...] “That made me fall back in love with cinema – the kind of cinema that was a space where you could be opinionated, and loud, and I’ve stuck by that,” Pugh said. “I think it’s far too easy for people in this industry to push you left and right. And I was lucky enough to discover when I was 19 what kind of a performer I wanted to be.”
sources.context: Relay of a Telegraph interview given during The Wonder press (late October 2022). Telegraph original is not reachable from this environment and was not opened. The pilot was Fox's Studio City (rising pop star opposite Eric McCormack); Fox passed on it, she returned to England, and the Lady Macbeth audition came 'two weeks later'. Note she did not refuse the changes: the show died. The 'stuck by that' resolution is retrospective self-report from six to seven years later. S03 relays the same interview and is not independent.

sources.title: How To Hit A Grand Slam: Florence Pugh On Her Breakout Year (Deadline Q&A)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, interviewed by Anthony D’Alessandro (Deadline)
sources.locator: Intro paragraph; answers on Fighting with My Family, Midsommar (Dani) and Little Women
sources.excerpt: Ever since Lady Macbeth and Family, I’ve been going back-to-back for about four years now. [...] In all honesty, I was scared, because I’d never come close to any sort of grief like that in my entire life. I didn’t know what that looked like, I didn’t know what that sounded like, and in a film where that is heavily based around anxiety and grief, it would almost be rude to wing it. [...] I imagined every single member of my family in a coffin, which got all the noises that you see in the film out of me. I’m sure many actors would say that’s totally ridiculous, but unfortunately, I can’t cry on cue. So, I had to really just destroy myself for an entire three months, but I was happy with the work. [...] Coming off Midsommar, Amy March in Little Women was the best therapy for me. She was amazing. I got to prance around in petticoats, and essentially flirt with Timothée Chalamet every day, and then punch and wrestle with all the sisters. It was great.
sources.context: Awards-season Q&A at the end of her 2019 breakout year. The earliest and least hindsight-shaped account of the Midsommar method; predates her 2023-2025 'abuse' framing. Deadline's own narration says 'Pugh got Aster and Gerwig to work it out a schedule so that she could walk from one film to the next' (writer's words). Opened in full; verified verbatim.

She’s a terrible person.’ But I get really arsey about that,” she says. “I can explain all the awful things that she does. sources.title: The Louis Theroux Podcast S6 E6: Florence Pugh (machine transcript)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, in conversation with Louis Theroux
sources.locator: Transcript timestamps 00:09:14-00:12:45 (arguing with directors; crying-scene retakes); 00:17:00-00:20:10 (Midsommar, Little Women, depression); 00:36:22-00:36:59 (being heard); 00:46:06-00:49:30 (privacy, Braff); 00:50:25-00:52:40 (past relationship, people-pleasing)
sources.excerpt: “sometimes at the beginning of my career, I hadn't quite figured out the relationship between director and actor yet, and I found myself arguing a lot. I mean, it's something that I still do in a softer way now [...] I just always felt so protective of the character that I was playing” / “women on set um it's a bit stickier you can't really be a problem because people will say that you're a nightmare [...] and when I'm in that state I kind of I'm a bit mushy so I'm like okay we'll do it again And my co-star went up to the director and said, don't do that, man. [...] I wouldn't have been able to have said that because that wouldn't have been received well.” / “Little Women was such a fun experience [...] so I think shelled all of that and then when I got home for Christmas I was so depressed I was like oh I think that's from Midsama and I didn't deal with it” / “I think when you're such a when you're such a bubbly person and you fill in a lot of energy for other people it's definitely I'm definitely the last person that I look after [...] I needed to be upbeat for everybody else and my issues, my worries, my pains weren't worthy of being spoken about. They weren't necessary to speak about because it would bring people down and we don't want that. [...] it's that people pleaser thing where you just try and keep things afloat without anybody else knowing that you're paddling for dear life.” / “I stood up for it and I stood up for him and I stood up for me just being allowed to do whatever the fuck I wanted to do [...] the one thing I can do is stop talking about that part of my life.”
sources.context: Long-form, unhurried conversation (about an hour), the most reflective source in the record. Machine transcript without speaker labels; the quoted lines are first-person answers and two segments were cross-checked against official YouTube clips by a research sub-agent. Do NOT attribute the ambiguous 'would you ever say no... no way can't do that' exchange near 00:11:11 to her. 'Shelled' is the transcript's rendering (likely 'shelved'). The people-pleasing passage follows her account of an unnamed past relationship that was 'causing you pain'; do not identify the partner. Opened and spot-verified verbatim.

sources.title: On the Eve of East of Eden, Florence Pugh Talks About Her Year of Rest and Relaxation (Vanity Fair cover story, October 2026 issue)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh, interviewed by Hillary Busis; with testimony from Zoe Kazan, Denis Villeneuve, Ari Aster, Ashley Park, Andrew Garfield, David Harbour
sources.locator: Full text; sections on Cathy Ames; Midsommar and protecting her space; siblings; Venice/Don’t Worry Darling; Finn Cole; social media; Gaza; producing and sets; lateness and rest
sources.excerpt: “I don’t know how to play characters without sympathizing with them. And I think I’ve tried to do my best after Midsommar to be fair to myself and also to be fair to the character,” she says. “I’ve learned over the years to know when enough is enough, when I’ve abused my state of mind or put my body through things that I shouldn’t. I now know how to protect my space.” [...] “I don’t like messy sets,” she says. “I want people to come to work and work, and enjoy that it’s a luxury to do this. When moods change on set, it’s because someone is preventing that from happening, and that’s what makes people feel like they haven’t been cared for.” [...] “I know that everybody in this industry has rises and falls. I’m not an idiot,” [...] “I wasn’t healthy, I wasn’t happy,” she says. “And I remember at the end of the year going, ‘Eww. I really want to change that. That’s not me.’” [...] “You don’t like that behavior? Change it now before it becomes comfortable.” [...] “I love packing,” she says. “I hate unpacking.” [...] “I don’t want to be a secret, but I also don’t want everything to be divulged,” [...] “But no, I was never scared of it”—even if she estimates she lost hundreds of thousands of followers for posting about the topic. [...] “I want to enter this decade and be like, We’re not gonna coast. We’re not gonna stay the same.” [...] “One of the things that I find most interesting about Florence is that she’s so lovely and warm and approachable and funny,” Kazan tells me. “And at the same time, she’s kind of all business on set. I walked away from our process not understanding any better than I did beforehand how she works.” [...] “There is something unapologetic about the way she inspires respect,” Denis Villeneuve, director of the Dune trilogy, says via email.
sources.context: Most recent long-form interview (conducted in London, July 2026, per research sub-agent; published online 2026-09-25 for the October 2026 'New Establishment' issue). Also contains: 'Oh, no. I feel like there's so much stuff we've covered...' when asked about Don't Worry Darling; asked how she met Finn Cole: 'No.'; 'I don't have that tic anymore. I guess maybe I'm not addicted to it anymore'; Ashley Park: 'She's a great chef, she's a great host, she's a great designer, she's a great planner. She has a confidence that's not egotistical'; Harbour: 'She gave me a lava lamp?'; on Cathy: 'I thought it was the most beautiful love letter to protecting her as a child. When I read that, I was like, ‘I can get behind her.’'; 'Emma Thomas, Amy Pascal. I gravitate toward women that command space.' The 'doesn't care about being adored by strangers' and 'control the narrative... without coming off as controlling' lines are the writer's interpretation. Opened directly in full via curl and verified verbatim.

sources.excerpt: For me, I’d say that I do have a feisty side, so I tried to incorporate that into Katherine as well. It was brilliant doing those scenes where the men would just imprison me sentence by sentence: it makes Katherine angry, and it made me angry. [...] I thought I crashed and burned, but then week by week I’d be given another reading.

sources.title: Florence Pugh Says 'Midsommar' Abuse Caused Depression for Six Months (Variety relay of The Louis Theroux Podcast)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh on The Louis Theroux Podcast; article by Zack Sharf (Variety)
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs quoting the podcast (Midsommar method, Little Women, depression)
sources.excerpt: “I just can’t exhaust myself like that because it has a knock-on effect,” Pugh said. “I think [‘Midsommar’] made me sad for like six months after and I didn’t know why I was depressed. I got back after shooting ‘Little Women,’ which was such a fun experience and obviously a completely different tone from ‘Midsommar,’ so I think shelved all of that. And then when I got home for Christmas, I was so depressed and I was like, ‘Oh, I think that’s from “Midsommar,”‘ and I didn’t deal with it and I probably shouldn’t do that again.” [...] “At the beginning, I just imagined hearing the news that one of my siblings had died, and then towards the middle of the shoot it was like, ‘Oh no, I actually needed to imagine the coffins.’ And then towards the end of the shoot, I actually was going to my whole family’s funeral.” [...] “I’d never done anything like that before and I was like, ‘OK, well here’s my opportunity. I need to give this a go.’ And I would just basically put myself through hell. But I don’t do that anymore. It really fucked me up.”
sources.context: Opened in the draft stage on 2026-10-04 via curl (WebFetch hits the tollbit redirect); published 2025-11-11T22:17Z. A professionally punctuated print transcription of the Theroux passages that S17 renders as machine text; it prints 'shelved' (S17 has 'shelled'). TheWrap's independent transcription (S61) matches word for word, and a YouTube news read-through also renders 'shelved'. Still a relay; the podcast audio itself was not reviewed.

sources.title: Florence Pugh reveals male co-star spoke up when director demanded more takes of difficult scene (Pearl & Dean Cinemas)
sources.speaker: Florence Pugh on The Louis Theroux Podcast; unbylined wire copy carried by Pearl & Dean Cinemas
sources.locator: Article body, paragraphs 3-7
sources.excerpt: The British actress admitted on The Louis Theroux Podcast that it can be “a bit stickier” for women to advocate for themselves on set in case they are branded “a nightmare”. [...] “And we did it maybe six times, and each time you have to start with no tears and then gear up. So you have to stay in it. And we got it, and the director wanted to go again. And when I’m in that state, I’m a bit mushy, so I’m like, ‘Okay, we’ll do it again.’ “My co-star went up to the director and said, ‘Don’t do that, man. Don’t put her through that. She’s got it. We got it. You’ve got the close-up, you’ve got the wide (shot), don’t do that.’” The Don’t Worry Darling star noted that the director agreed with her co-star “straight away”, and she realised that if she’d spoken up for herself in the same way, it “wouldn’t have been received well”. Pugh did not name the co-star or the film.
sources.context: Wire copy (datePublished 2025-11-11T10:51Z); identical text runs on Film-News.co.uk. Opened via curl in the draft stage. Its intimacy-coordinator quotes match the official Louis Theroux YouTube clip captions (S59) word for word, which supports the accuracy of the transcription. Confirms the retakes passage that S17 has only as machine text. 'A bit stickier' and 'a nightmare' are short quoted fragments inside the writer's paraphrase.

It does not contain the 'people pleaser... paddling for dear life' sentence. The same article reports self-injury during the unnamed relationship; that material must not be used.

claims.claim: In December 2019 she told Deadline: 'unfortunately, I can't cry on cue. So, I had to really just destroy myself for an entire three months, but I was happy with the work.'
claims.passage: "unfortunately, I can't cry on cue. So, I had to really just destroy myself for an entire three months, but I was happy with the work."
claims.inference: Consistent account across 2019 (Deadline, TheWrap) and 2025 (Theroux). Shows willingness to enter pain deliberately for the work.
claims.alternative: This is professional method under a director's demand, not a life choice about her own pain; it complicates any claim that she avoids pain. Shoot length is given as 'three months' (2019) and 'like four months' (2023).

claims.claim: On the Theroux podcast (November 2025) she described escalating the Midsommar method from imagining a sibling's death to imagining coffins to 'going to my whole family's funeral'.
claims.passage: By the middle of the shoot, "I actually needed to imagine the coffins." By the end, "I actually was going to my whole family's funeral."
claims.inference: Print transcription (Variety) of the podcast; consistent with her 2019 Deadline account of imagining her family in coffins (S04).
claims.alternative: Retrospective account told six years later; craft method under a director, not a life choice about her own pain.

claims.claim: She moved from the Midsommar shoot to Little Women with little gap (three days by one account, two weeks by another).
claims.passage: From there she went almost straight to Greta Gerwig's _Little Women_, where she played Amy March.
claims.inference: Deadline says she got the directors to arrange the schedule; TheWrap quotes "two weeks previous"; S17 gives about three days.
claims.alternative: Back-to-back scheduling is common for in-demand actors and was a career decision, not necessarily an emotional one.

claims.claim: In December 2019 she called Amy March 'the best therapy for me' after Midsommar.
claims.passage: "Coming off Midsommar, Amy March in Little Women was the best therapy for me," she told Deadline.
claims.inference: Contemporaneous framing of the switch as a cure.
claims.alternative: Awards-season promotion for Little Women invites a positive framing.

claims.claim: She described Little Women as getting 'to prance around in petticoats, and essentially flirt with Timothée Chalamet every day'.
claims.passage: She got to "prance around in petticoats" and flirt on camera with
claims.inference: Light, playful register in the 2019 account.
claims.alternative: Promotional colour; paraphrased in part.

claims.claim: She told TheWrap that 'playing and cuddling everyone on the set' was 'the perfect way to balance who I was two weeks previous.'
claims.passage: Being on that set, "playing and cuddling everyone," was "the perfect way to balance who I was two weeks previous."
claims.inference: Contemporaneous: distress balanced by play and company.
claims.alternative: Promotional; one interview.

claims.claim: In November 2025 she said Little Women 'was such a fun experience and obviously a completely different tone from Midsommar, so I think shelved all of that. And then when I got home for Christmas, I was so depressed.'
claims.passage: _Little Women_ "was such a fun experience and obviously a completely different tone from 'Midsommar,' so I think shelved all of that. And then when I got home for Christmas, I was so depressed."
claims.inference: The same sequence told twice: in 2019 as a cure through play and company (C53, C55), in 2025 as pain set aside unprocessed that returned later. This suggests a pattern of meeting distress by moving to something lighter rather than staying with it.
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-diagnosis; the scheduling was a career necessity. The wording is now confirmed by two print transcriptions (Variety, TheWrap), which print 'shelved'; the audio itself was not reviewed.

claims.claim: She said in November 2025 that Midsommar 'made me sad for like six months after and I didn't know why I was depressed.'
claims.passage: "I think ['Midsommar'] made me sad for like six months after and I didn't know why I was depressed."
claims.inference: Two print transcriptions agree.
claims.alternative: Self-report of mood years later; not a clinical claim and should not be presented as one.

claims.claim: Greta Gerwig told TheWrap in 2019: 'There is something about her that can't be knocked down or overtaken.'
claims.passage: "There is something about her that can't be knocked down or overtaken," Gerwig said in 2019
claims.inference: Named director testimony of strength.
claims.alternative: Promotional quote about a star she directed.

claims.claim: The article's thesis: across contexts she meets pain with motion and lightness and names the cost later.
claims.passage: When pain arrives, she moves toward something lighter and faster, and names the cost later.
claims.inference: Drawn from the convergent sequence in C08, C18, C09, C15, C36 and C14.
claims.alternative: Each item alone has an ordinary explanation (craft, normal processing, lockdown, adolescence); the claim rests on the convergence, and the Eight and Two alternatives are argued in the article.

claims.passage: Pugh was born on January 3, 1996, in Oxford, England

claims.passage: She is also an executive producer of _East of Eden_, Zoe Kazan's 2026 Netflix series, in which she plays Cathy Ames.

claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: The source base is structurally tilted: almost everything is press-tour or cover-story material in which candour, warmth and 'no-BS' defiance are part of the Florence Pugh brand ('Fans have come to expect this kind of no-BS fiery candor', Harper's Bazaar's writer, 2022; 'she's figured out a way to control the narrative around her without coming off as controlling', Vanity Fair's writer, 2026). The two most reflective sources (Reign 2025, Theroux 2025) are long-form podcasts where she volunteers costs and people-pleasing.
claims.passage: Nearly everything public about her comes from press tours and cover stories, where candor and warmth are part of the brand.
claims.inference: Weight long-form, unprompted reflection above cover-story framing; treat writers' characterisations as interpretation.
claims.alternative: Even the podcasts are promotional appearances; the record cannot see her private conduct.

claims.claim: Leading type hypothesis: Type 7, medium confidence; Type 8 strongest alternative; Type 2 live third reading.
claims.passage: Florence Pugh most likely fits Enneagram Type 7, the Enthusiast, at medium confidence.
claims.inference: See type_hypothesis; argued in the article against Types 8 and 2.
claims.alternative: Contested typing: fan sites call her an 8 (S40); collaborator testimony supports 8 (C32); her people-pleasing self-report supports 2 (C09, C30).

claims.claim: Parents Deborah (dancer) and Clinton Pugh (restaurateur); siblings Toby Sebastian (actor and musician), Arabella Gibbins (actor) and younger sister Rafaela.
claims.passage: Her mother, Deborah, is a dancer, and her father, Clinton Pugh, a restaurateur. She has an older brother, the actor and musician Toby Sebastian, an older sister, the actor Arabella Gibbins, and a younger sister, Rafaela.
claims.inference: Consistent across Wikipedia, Vogue 2020 and Vanity Fair 2026.
claims.alternative: Do not publish Rafaela's field of work; Pugh withheld it in Vanity Fair 2026.

claims.claim: As a small child she had tracheomalacia and was in and out of hospital; the family moved to southern Spain when she was about three and returned to Oxford when she was about six.
claims.passage: As a small child she had tracheomalacia, a weak windpipe, and was in and out of hospital; the family moved to southern Spain when she was about three and came back to Oxford when she was about six.
claims.inference: Medical history and the Spain move are consistent across Wikipedia, Vogue 2023 and Vanity Fair 2026. Her own framing explicitly refuses a wound narrative.
claims.alternative: Do not present the illness as a formative wound or causal origin of her temperament; she rejects that reading and no source supports it. The voice is a physical trait, not a personality signal.

claims.claim: She told Vogue in 2023: 'I never want this to be a sob story, because it's never been a story in my life.'
claims.passage: "I never want this to be a sob story," she told Vogue in 2023, "because it's never been a story in my life."
claims.inference: She explicitly refuses a wound narrative; the article draws nothing about type from the illness.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: Vogue 2020: 'We're a big eating family... It's all big and loving and homey'; the writer notes she grew up in a family of hosts.
claims.passage: "We're a big eating family," she told Vogue in 2020. "It's all big and loving and homey."
claims.inference: Family culture of food and hosting.
claims.alternative: Family restaurant culture explains much of her hosting; supports both Type 2 and Type 7 readings.

claims.claim: Of a childhood school nativity she told The Guardian (2018): 'It was the first time I knew the power of being on stage... I have complete control.' I still feel that now.'
claims.passage: "It was the first time I knew the power of being on stage. I remember thinking, 'Oh God, they're waiting for me, they're listening to everything I say and I have complete control.' I still feel that now,"
claims.inference: A consistent, vivid early pleasure in performance, in holding a room and in the 'power' and 'control' of an audience's attention.
claims.alternative: Childhood performers of every type say this. 'Power' and 'complete control' fit Type 8 or Type 3 as well as Type 7. The BBC Radio 4 versions (S43) are machine-transcribed and are not quoted.

claims.claim: The Observer, December 2014 (age 18): 'Throughout my life, I've been that annoying kid on every stage at school, in every talent contest.'
claims.passage: At 18 she called herself "that annoying kid on every stage at school, in every talent contest."
claims.inference: Early, pre-fame self-description as a compulsive performer.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecating interview humour.

claims.claim: The childhood performance record does not discriminate between Types 7, 8 and 3.
claims.passage: "Complete control" sounds as much like an Eight, or a Three holding an audience, as a Seven chasing the thrill of the live moment.
claims.inference: Honest limit on the childhood evidence.
claims.alternative: None; this is a statement of what the evidence cannot show.

claims.claim: At 17 she nearly did not send a tape for The Falling's open audition because of what her brother's career had taught her ('that's not how you're going to get a part'); her mother persuaded her ('it's kind of a free go'), and she was cast.
claims.passage: "My brother was in the industry, and I knew that's not how you're going to get a part, handing in a three-minute tape." Her mother talked her into it: "We know you aren't going to get it, but this is something you want to do with your life, so it's kind of a free go."
claims.inference: A protective pessimism about hope followed by full commitment once in the room. Director Carol Morley says she 'quickly knew she was Abbie'.
claims.alternative: Accounts of the route in differ: tape at home (S49, S43), leaflet at school (S46), the agent emailing schools (S47), or Morley visiting her boarding school (S45). Treat the details as approximate; the hesitancy rests on retrospective self-report.

claims.claim: The Observer, December 2014: 'I do like a bit of danger... Guns, cars, running, bullets. I'm up for it.'
claims.passage: "I do like a bit of danger," she told The Observer. "Guns, cars, running, bullets. I'm up for it."
claims.inference: Thrill-seeking predates the stunt record (C13, C14) by a decade.
claims.alternative: Light, genre-preference remarks by a teenager promoting an art film; useful only as a pattern marker.

claims.claim: The Observer, December 2014: 'It's a bit of a fluke.' She repeated the worry in 2017 and 2022.
claims.passage: And of her break: "It's a bit of a fluke."
claims.inference: Recurring self-doubt under the confident persona, consistent with her own statement that confidence came later (C36).
claims.alternative: Modesty is a British interview norm, and calling an early break a fluke is a common humility move; it may also reflect a Type 6 or Type 3 worry. Not decisive.

claims.claim: At 19 she was cast as the lead in Fox's pilot Studio City; in 2022 she said its makers tried to change 'my weight, my look, the shape of my face, the shape of my eyebrows' and 'I felt I'd made a massive mistake'. Fox passed, and she auditioned for Lady Macbeth two weeks later.
claims.passage: In 2022 she told The Telegraph, as relayed by Variety, that the people behind it tried to change "my weight, my look, the shape of my face, the shape of my eyebrows," and that "I felt I'd made a massive mistake."
claims.inference: A retrospective origin story (told in 2022) that frames her later stance as a refusal to be reshaped. The pilot was not picked up; she did not have to refuse anything at the time.
claims.alternative: Hindsight narrative useful to a brand built on candor; the Telegraph original was not opened and both relays (Variety, W) derive from it. The stated value is freedom from being 'pushed left and right' (fits 7 or 8), not dominance.

claims.claim: Of Lady Macbeth (told 2022): 'That made me fall back in love with cinema – the kind of cinema that was a space where you could be opinionated, and loud, and I've stuck by that... I think it's far too easy for people in this industry to push you left and right.'
claims.passage: "That made me fall back in love with cinema – the kind of cinema that was a space where you could be opinionated, and loud, and I've stuck by that," she said. "I think it's far too easy for people in this industry to push you left and right."
claims.inference: Retrospective origin story; the stated value is freedom from being pushed 'left and right'.
claims.alternative: Telegraph original paywalled and not opened; both relays (S02, S03) derive from it. Hindsight narrative useful to a candid brand; she did not have to refuse anything at the time (the pilot died).

claims.claim: Grazia, April 2017 (age 21): 'I don't like being told how to do things... it makes Katherine angry, and it made me angry.'
claims.passage: "I don't like being told how to do things," she told Grazia in 2017, describing scenes where the men around her _Lady Macbeth_ character confine her: "it makes Katherine angry, and it made me angry."
claims.inference: Anti-constraint is her oldest stated value, voiced at 19 to 21 before her persona was a brand, and it lines up with her later 'push you left and right' and 'freedom' language (C04, C18).
claims.alternative: Resisting being told what to do fits Type 7 (freedom from limits) and Type 8 (autonomy, refusing control) about equally; the teenage-school context is ordinary adolescent friction.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the stated object of her defiance is freedom from being told, pushed or reshaped.
claims.passage: What her defiance names, from 19 on, is being told, pushed and boxed in.
claims.inference: Convergent wording from 2017 ('told how to do things', 'told no'), 2022 ('push you left and right'), 2023 ('the freedom that people are scared of') and 2025 ('have things just happen to me').
claims.alternative: Resisting being told what to do fits Type 8 (autonomy) nearly as well as Type 7; this is a tilt, not proof.

claims.claim: AP, July 2019: 'To get it perfect, I knew, would be so exhilarating and the payoff would be a fantastic feeling — which it was.' Her account of Midsommar's cost changed over the following six years.
claims.passage: "To get it perfect, I knew, would be so exhilarating and the payoff would be a fantastic feeling — which it was,"
claims.inference: A dated arc of reinterpretation, moving from thrill to cost to boundary. The thrill framing came first and the pain was named years later.
claims.alternative: The shift may reflect changing industry vocabulary about wellbeing and the incentives of later press cycles, not a change in her underlying pattern.

claims.claim: Off Menu podcast, March 2023 (via Variety): 'I think by the end I probably, most definitely abused my own self in order to get that performance.'
claims.passage: she said she "most definitely abused my own self in order to get that performance"
claims.inference: Middle step of the dated arc of reinterpretation (C07).
claims.alternative: Relay; podcast audio not reviewed. Comedy-podcast setting.

claims.claim: November 2025: 'But I don't do that anymore. It really fucked me up.'
claims.passage: In November 2025: "But I don't do that anymore. It really fucked me up."
claims.inference: Late step in the arc.
claims.alternative: Retrospective; therapeutic vocabulary common in recent press cycles.

claims.claim: Vanity Fair 2026: 'I now know how to protect my space.'
claims.passage: "I now know how to protect my space."
claims.inference: Latest step: cost turned into a boundary.
claims.alternative: Cover-story framing.

claims.claim: Reign (January 2025): she is proud of the Midsommar performance, 'so I don't regret it'.
claims.passage: She has also said she is proud of the performance, "so I don't regret it"

type_hypothesis.against: Three bodies of evidence push against Type 7. Type 8: Shortland, Gerwig, Johansson and Villeneuve describe steel, refusal to yield and an unapologetic presence (C32, C57, C83, C84); she calls herself 'a bit of a big mouth' (C03), forces physical commitments past institutional caution (C13, C85, C86), defends a partner and causes publicly at real cost (C16, C88, C89, C26, C90, C91, C92) and wants producing power and orderly sets (C34). Type 2: her own words for her most costly habit are a Helper's ('the last person that I look after', 'good for everybody else', C09; 'people pleaser', C76, machine transcript only), she says she loves 'looking after people' (C30, C104), was a second mother to her youngest sister (C105), and is described as a host (C31, C106); her case for rest is about being kinder to others (C11). The childhood 'complete control' pleasure in performing (C45) reads as 8 or 3 as easily as 7. And she moves toward pain in the work (C06, C51, C12, C111, C112, C113, C24). Circumstance explains much of the 7-looking surface: back-to-back scheduling in peak demand (C52), a gendered constraint on pushback she names herself (C95, C97), a candid brand (C43), and post-breakup therapeutic vocabulary (C29).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: On the Type 8 reading the through-line is refusal to be controlled or reshaped, plus protection of the vulnerable. 'Complete control' over a silent audience at a school nativity (C45); 'I don't like being told how to do things... it made me angry' at 21 (C46); 'push you left and right' after Studio City (C04, C65); 'a bit of a big mouth' (C03); five collaborators over seven years describing force and steel (C32, C57, C83, C84); persistence against Marvel's insurance caution and her director's resistance (C13, C85, C86); public, profane defiance of body-shamers and abusers (C73, C88); 'I'll always defend people that I love' (C89); rage and audience loss over Gaza and the Cornell case (C26, C90, C92); executive-producer power and 'women that command space' (C34). On this reading the people-pleasing line describes one painful relationship (C29), and her softness on set is a learned gendered strategy she names herself (C95, C97).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What she does with her own pain, and what her pushback defends. (1) Her stated reason for hiding pain is that it 'would bring people down' (C09, C78), not fear of appearing weak or controlled; the same move recurs in unrelated contexts and years: Little Women as 'the best therapy' after Midsommar, then depression at Christmas she hadn't dealt with (C53, C55, C08, C56); dancing and cooking to 'keep moving' in lockdown (C79, C15); teenage 'quick fixes' (C36, C80); and leading with 'not a wink of me was nervous' before naming the hurt two years later (C71, C18, C75). Note: the print relay (S58) has 'good for everybody else' where the machine transcript has 'upbeat'; the argument does not rest on that word. (2) In her most detailed on-set standoff she went along ('I'm a bit mushy') until a male co-star intervened (C23, C96, C97); she gives a gendered explanation and says she can make herself heard (C95, C98), so this supports rather than decides (C99). (3) Her defiance names freedom: being 'told how to do things' (C46), 'push you left and right' (C65), 'the freedom that people are scared of' (C74), 'I don't want to have things just happen to me any more' (C28); her firmest statements tend to end in a joke and an exit ('Well, don't', 'Tut tut tut', 'let that one sit', C73, C93, C102, C100). Shortland's 'will not back down' (C32) and the Cornell rage (C92) fit the Eight better, and the article shows both. Against Type 2 the discriminator is weaker: what she describes chasing is beginnings (C10, C107, C121), she rejects approval as her engine (C109), though C44 cuts the other way (C108, C110).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: (1) Her attraction to pain in the work: the Midsommar method (C06, C51), 'I sometimes prefer [acting in pain]' and 'my duty to play human and ugly' (C12, C111), roles that terrify her (C112), six years on Cathy Ames (C113, C24). Craft may explain it, or the 7 reading is incomplete; fear-seeking choices could also suggest a counterphobic Six. (2) Moral anger and audience loss over Gaza and the Cornell case (C26, C90, C92) fit 8 or 2 better than 7. (3) The people-pleasing self-report (C09, C76) and her love of looking after people (C30, C104) remain the strongest Type 2 evidence. (4) Her 2024-2026 turn toward home and security ('safety, family, a home and security', 'solid and safe and sturdy', C114, C115, C25) could be maturation, a stable relationship or a security motive. (5) Collaborators find her process opaque (C33), and the record is almost entirely promotional (C43). Wing and subtype are left unassigned.
